danish.title: Ellevte bog (1812) — Kapitel 28
paragraphs: Pierre, der havde besluttet, at han indtil gennemførelsen af sin plan hverken ville afsløre sin identitet eller sit kendskab til fransk, stod ved gangdørens halvåbne dør med den hensigt at skjule sig, så snart franskmændene kom ind. Men franskmændene kom ind, og stadig trak Pierre sig ikke tilbage — en uimodståelig nysgerrighed holdt ham dér.

De var to. Den ene var en officer — en høj, soldatermæssig, flot mand — den anden tilsyneladende menig eller oppasser, solbrændt, lille og mager, med indfaldne kinder og et sløvt udtryk. Officeren gik forrest, støttende sig på en stok og lettere haltende. Da han var kommet nogle skridt, standsede han, da han tilsyneladende havde besluttet, at dette var et godt kvarter, vendte sig mod soldaterne ved indgangen og beordrede med høj kommandostemme, at hestene skulle staldtes. Derpå strøg officeren sin moustache med en elegant bevægelse af albuen og berørte let sin hat.
»Bonjour, la compagnie!« * sagde han muntert, smilende og seende sig om.
* »Goddag, hele selskabet!«
Ingen svarede.
»Vous êtes le bourgeois?« * spurgte officeren Gerasim.
* »Er det Dem, der er herren i huset?«
Gerasim stirrede på officeren med et forskrækket og spørgende blik.

»Quartier, quartier, logement!« sagde officeren og kiggede ned på den lille mand med et nedladende og godmodigt smil. »Les français sont de bons enfants. Que diable! Voyons! Ne nous fâchons pas, mon vieux!« * tilføjede han og klappede den forskrækkede og tavse Gerasim på skulderen. »Nå, er der ingen her, der taler fransk?« Han kiggede rundt og mødte Pierres øjne. Pierre trak sig væk fra døren.
* »Kvarter, kvarter, logi! Franskmændene er gode drenge. For pokker! Kom nu! Lad os ikke blive sure, gamle ven!«
Officeren vendte sig igen til Gerasim og bad ham vise ham husets værelser.
»Herren, ikke her — forstår ikke... mig, dig...« sagde Gerasim og forsøgte at gøre sine ord mere forståelige ved at forvride dem.

Stadig smilende bredte den franske officer sine hænder ud foran Gerasims næse for at antyde, at han heller ikke forstod ham, og gik, haltende, hen til døren, hvor Pierre stod. Pierre ønskede at gå sin vej og skjule sig, men i det øjeblik så han Makar Aleksejevitj dukke op ved den åbne køkkendør med pistolen i hånden. Med en gal mands list stirrede Makar Aleksejevitj på franskmanden, løftede sin pistol og sigtede.

»Enter dem!« brølede den berusede mand og forsøgte at trykke på aftrækkeren. Da officeren hørte råbet, vendte han sig om, og i samme øjeblik kastede Pierre sig over drukkenbolten. Netop da Pierre greb fat i pistolen og slog den til side, fik Makar Aleksejevitj endelig fingrene på aftrækkeren, et øredøvende skud lød, og alle blev indhyllet i en sky af røg. Franskmanden blev bleg og styrtede hen mod døren.
Pierre glemte sin hensigt om at skjule sit kendskab til fransk, rev pistolen til sig, kastede den og løb hen til officeren og tiltalte ham på fransk.
»De er ikke såret?« spurgte han.

»Det tror jeg ikke,« svarede franskmanden og mærkede efter. »Men det var lige ved denne gang,« tilføjede han og pegede på det beskadigede puds på væggen. »Hvem er den mand?« sagde han og kiggede strengt på Pierre.
»Åh, jeg er virkelig fortvivlet over det skete,« sagde Pierre hurtigt og glemte helt den rolle, han havde tiltænkt sig. »Han er en ulykkelig sindsforvirret, der ikke vidste, hvad han gjorde.«
Officeren gik hen til Makar Aleksejevitj og greb ham i kraven.
Makar Aleksejevitj stod med åben mund og svajede, som om han var ved at falde i søvn, lænet mod væggen.

»Bandit! Det skal du bøde for,« sagde franskmanden og slap ham. »Vi franskmænd er nådige efter sejren, men vi tilgiver ikke forrædere,« tilføjede han med et blik af dyster værdighed og en fin, energisk gestus.

Pierre fortsatte på fransk med at overtale officeren til ikke at drage den berusede idiot til ansvar. Franskmanden lyttede tavst med det samme dystre udtryk, men vendte sig pludselig mod Pierre med et smil. I nogle sekunder kiggede han på ham i tavshed. Hans flotte ansigt antog et melodramatisk blidt udtryk, og han rakte hånden ud.
»De har reddet mit liv. De er franskmand,« sagde han.

For en franskmand var denne slutning uomtvistelig. Kun en franskmand kunne udføre en stor dåd, og at redde hans liv — livet af M. Ramballe, kaptajn ved det 13. lette regiment — var uden tvivl en meget stor dåd.
Men hvor uomtvistelig end denne konklusion og officerens overbevisning var, følte Pierre det nødvendigt at korrigere ham.
»Jeg er russer,« sagde han hurtigt.

»Snik snak! Fortæl det til andre,« sagde officeren og viftede med fingeren foran sin næse, smilende. »De skal nok fortælle mig alt om det om lidt. Jeg er henrykt over at møde en landsmand. Nå, og hvad skal vi gøre med denne mand?« tilføjede han og henvendte sig til Pierre som til en broder.

Selv om Pierre ikke var franskmand, kunne han, efter at have modtaget menneskets ypperste betegnelse, ikke afvise den, sagde officerens blik og tone. Som svar på hans sidste spørgsmål forklarede Pierre igen, hvem Makar Aleksejevitj var, og hvordan den berusede idiot lige inden deres ankomst havde grebet den ladede pistol, som de ikke havde haft tid til at tage fra ham, og bad officeren om at lade gerningen gå ustraffet hen.
Franskmanden spilede brystet op og gjorde en majestætisk gestus med armen.

»De har reddet mit liv! De er franskmand. De beder om hans benådning? Jeg tilstår den. Før den mand bort!« sagde han hurtigt og energisk og tog armen på Pierre, som han havde forfremmet til franskmand for at have reddet hans liv, og gik med ham ind i værelset.
Soldaterne i gården, der havde hørt skuddet, kom ind i gangen og spurgte, hvad der var sket, og udtrykte deres vilje til at straffe de skyldige, men officeren standsede dem strengt.
»I bliver kaldt, når I er ønsket,« sagde han.
Soldaterne gik ud igen, og oppasseren, der i mellemtiden havde haft tid til at besøge køkkenet, kom hen til sin officer.
»Kaptajn, der er suppe og et lammekølle i køkkenet,« sagde han. »Skal jeg servere?«
»Ja, og noget vin,« svarede kaptajnen.

english.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 28
paragraphs: Pierre, having decided that until he carried out his plan he would reveal neither his identity nor his knowledge of French, stood at the half-open corridor door, intending to hide as soon as the French entered. But the French came in, and still Pierre did not retreat—an irresistible curiosity kept him there.

There were two of them. One was an officer—a tall, soldierly, handsome man—the other evidently a private or an orderly, sunburned, short, and thin, with sunken cheeks and a dull expression. The officer walked in front, leaning on a stick and limping slightly. When he had advanced a few steps, he stopped, apparently having decided these were good quarters, turned to the soldiers standing at the entrance, and in a loud voice ordered them to stable the horses. Having done that, the officer, lifting his elbow with a smart gesture, stroked his mustache and lightly touched his hat.
"Good day, everybody!" he said gaily, smiling and looking about him.
* "Good day, everybody!"
No one answered.
"Are you the master here?" the officer asked Gerasim.
* "Are you the master here?"
Gerasim gazed at the officer with an alarmed and questioning look.

"Quarters, quarters, lodgings!" said the officer, looking down at the little man with a condescending, good-natured smile. "The French are good fellows. Come now! Don't let's be cross, old fellow!" he added, clapping the scared and silent Gerasim on the shoulder. "Well, does no one speak French in this establishment?" he asked again in French, looking around and meeting Pierre's eyes. Pierre moved away from the door.
* "Quarters, quarters, lodgings! The French are good fellows. What the devil! There, don't let us be cross, old fellow!"
Again the officer turned to Gerasim and asked him to show him the rooms in the house.
"Master, not here—don't understand... me, you..." said Gerasim, trying to make his words more comprehensible by distorting them.

Still smiling, the French officer spread out his hands before Gerasim's nose, indicating that he didn't understand him either, and moved, limping, to the door where Pierre was standing. Pierre wanted to go away and hide, but at that moment he saw Makar Alexeevich appearing at the open kitchen door with the pistol in his hand. With a madman's cunning, Makar Alexeevich eyed the Frenchman, raised his pistol, and took aim.

"Board them!" yelled the tipsy man, trying to pull the trigger. Hearing the yell, the officer turned around, and at the same moment Pierre threw himself at the drunkard. Just as Pierre grabbed and knocked up the pistol, Makar Alexeevich finally got his fingers on the trigger—there was a deafening report, and everything was enveloped in a cloud of smoke. The Frenchman turned pale and rushed to the door.
Forgetting his intention of concealing his knowledge of French, Pierre snatched away the pistol, threw it down, ran up to the officer, and addressed him in French.
"You are not wounded?" he asked.

"I think not," answered the Frenchman, feeling himself over. "But I've had a lucky escape this time," he added, pointing to the damaged plaster on the wall. "Who is that man?" he asked, looking sternly at Pierre.
"Oh, I am truly sorry about what has happened," said Pierre quickly, completely forgetting the role he had meant to play. "He is an unfortunate madman who did not know what he was doing."
The officer went up to Makar Alexeevich and took him by the collar.
Makar Alexeevich was standing with parted lips, swaying as if about to fall asleep, leaning against the wall.

"Scoundrel! You shall pay for this," said the Frenchman, letting go of him. "We French are merciful after victory, but we do not pardon traitors," he added, with a look of gloomy dignity and a fine, dramatic gesture.

Pierre continued, in French, to persuade the officer not to hold the drunken imbecile accountable. The Frenchman listened in silence with the same gloomy expression, but suddenly turned to Pierre with a smile. For a few seconds he looked at him in silence. His handsome face assumed a melodramatically gentle expression and he held out his hand.
"You have saved my life. You are French," said he.

For a Frenchman, that conclusion was indisputable. Only a Frenchman could perform a great deed, and to save his life—the life of Monsieur Ramballe, captain of the 13th Light Regiment—was undoubtedly a very great deed.
But however certain that conclusion and the officer's conviction based upon it, Pierre felt it necessary to correct him.
"I am Russian," he said quickly.

"Oh, come now! Tell that to others," said the officer, waving his finger before his nose and smiling. "You shall tell me all about that later. I am delighted to meet a compatriot. Well, and what are we to do with this man?" he added, addressing Pierre as a brother.

Even if Pierre were not a Frenchman, having once received that loftiest of human titles, he could not renounce it—the officer's look and tone said as much. In reply to his last question, Pierre again explained who Makar Alexeevich was and how just before their arrival the drunken imbecile had seized the loaded pistol which they had not had time to take from him, and he begged the officer to let the deed go unpunished.
The Frenchman puffed out his chest and made a grand gesture with his arm.

"You have saved my life! You are French. You ask his pardon? I grant it. Lead that man away!" he said quickly and energetically, and taking the arm of Pierre—whom he had promoted to the status of Frenchman for saving his life—he went with him into the room.
The soldiers in the yard, hearing the shot, came into the corridor asking what had happened, and expressed their readiness to punish the culprit, but the officer sternly stopped them.
"You will be called when you are wanted," he said.
The soldiers went out again, and the orderly, who had meanwhile had time to visit the kitchen, came up to his officer.
"Captain, there is soup and a leg of mutton in the kitchen," said he. "Shall I serve them up?"
"Yes, and some wine," answered the captain.
